questions.question: How do you set up a Mockito test class in JUnit 5?
questions.title: Mockito Test Setup JUnit 5 | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: Add @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) to the test class, use @Mock to declare mock dependencies, and @InjectMocks for the class under test. MockitoExtension initializes all annotated mocks before each test method runs automatically.

interviewer_intent.testing: Can you write a runnable Mockito test class from scratch without looking up documentation?
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting @ExtendWith and getting NullPointerException when mocks are not initialized.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show a complete working test class with all three annotations in proper context and explain the initialization flow.

sections.title: Setting Up Mockito Tests in JUnit 5
sections.content:
Mockito in JUnit 5 relies on the **MockitoExtension** to wire up your test infrastructure. You annotate your test class with **@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)** so JUnit knows to hand off mock initialization to Mockito before each test runs. Inside the class, you mark dependencies with **@Mock** to create fake objects, and the class you're testing with **@InjectMocks** so Mockito automatically injects those mocks into it.

Think of it like assembling a car on a test bench: @Mock creates the fake engine and wheels, @InjectMocks builds the car frame, and MockitoExtension bolts them all together before you turn the ignition. This setup ensures every test starts with fresh, isolated mocks—no leftover state from previous tests polluting your results.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|The Extension|~Wires Mockito to JUnit 5|the ExtendWith annotation|MockitoExtension class|runs before each test
blue|The Annotations|~Declare your doubles|the Mock annotation|the InjectMocks annotation|auto-initialised
emerald|Strictness|~Catches mistakes|strict stubs by default|flags unused stubs|cleaner tests

sections.title: Complete Mockito Test Class Setup
When to Use This Setup
sections.content: Use **@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)** in every pure unit test where you're testing a single class in isolation from its dependencies. This is your default setup for service layer tests where you mock repositories, external APIs, or other services. For example, testing an OrderService that depends on a PaymentGateway and EmailService—you mock both dependencies and verify the OrderService logic without hitting real payment systems or sending actual emails. Don't use this in integration tests where you want real Spring beans; there you'd use @SpringBootTest with @MockBean instead.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Forgetting @ExtendWith**: Writing @Mock and @InjectMocks but not adding @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) to the class header—mocks stay null and you get NullPointerException on the first method call.
- **Wrong JUnit version**: Using MockitoJUnitRunner (JUnit 4 syntax) in a JUnit 5 project—it doesn't work and fails at runtime with cryptic errors.
- **Manual initialization confusion**: Calling MockitoAnnotations.openMocks(this) in @BeforeEach when you already have @ExtendWith—you're initializing mocks twice, which is redundant and can cause subtle test issues.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)**: JUnit 5 extension that initializes Mockito mocks before each test method runs
- **@Mock**: Creates a mock object for a dependency—all methods return null/0/false by default until you stub them
- **@InjectMocks**: Creates the real class under test and injects all @Mock dependencies into it automatically
- **MockitoExtension**: Enables strict stubbing by default, which fails tests if you declare unused stubs
- **Lifecycle**: MockitoExtension runs before @BeforeEach, so mocks are ready when your setup code executes
- **Isolation**: Each test gets fresh mocks—no state leaks between tests even if they run in parallel
- **Spring difference**: For Spring context tests use @MockBean instead of @Mock, but keep the same @InjectMocks pattern

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: To set up a Mockito test in JUnit 5, you start by adding the @ExtendWith annotation with MockitoExtension.class at the top of your test class. This tells JUnit to let Mockito handle the mock lifecycle. Inside the class, you use @Mock to create fake versions of your dependencies—like repositories or external services. Then you use @InjectMocks on the class you're actually testing, and Mockito automatically injects those mocks into it. For example, if I'm testing an OrderService that needs a PaymentGateway and an InventoryRepository, I'd mark both of those as @Mock and the OrderService as @InjectMocks. When the test runs, MockitoExtension initializes all the mocks before my test method starts, so everything's wired up and ready to go. One thing freshers often miss—if you forget the @ExtendWith annotation, your mocks will be null and you'll get a NullPointerException the moment you try to use them. The extension is what actually creates the mock objects; without it, the annotations are just decorations that do nothing. That's the core setup—those three annotations in the right places, and you've got a working Mockito test.

questions.question: How do you create a mock manually without annotations in Mockito?
questions.title: Mockito.mock() Manual Creation | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: Use Mockito.mock(ClassName.class) to create a mock programmatically without annotations. This gives you the same mock object as @Mock but inline. Use it when you need to create mocks dynamically, work with generic types, or generate mocks in helper methods outside the test class lifecycle.

interviewer_intent.testing: Do you know both annotation-based and programmatic Mockito styles, and when each is appropriate?
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Only knowing @Mock annotation and being stuck when annotations don't work, like with generic types or dynamic mock creation.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain concrete scenarios where manual mock creation is necessary: parameterized tests, factory methods, or mocking List<String> where the type parameter matters.

sections.title: Creating Mocks Programmatically with Mockito.mock()
sections.content:
The **Mockito.mock(Class.class)** method creates mock objects on demand without needing annotations or the MockitoExtension lifecycle. You call it directly in your test code—usually in @BeforeEach or inside individual test methods—and get back a fully functional mock immediately. It's the same mock you'd get from @Mock, just created manually.

Think of it like the difference between declaring a variable at the class level versus inside a method: @Mock is the field declaration approach, while Mockito.mock() is the local variable approach. You need the programmatic style when **annotations can't express what you want**: mocking generic types like List<String> where the type parameter matters, creating mocks inside loops or factory methods, generating mocks conditionally based on test parameters, or working in plain Java classes without JUnit's annotation processing. The mock() method gives you complete control over when and how mocks are created, at the cost of slightly more verbose code.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Manual Mock|~No annotations|Mockito.mock(Class)|returns a fake|assign to a field
blue|When to Use|~Outside JUnit lifecycle|parameterised setups|local one-off mocks|dynamic types
emerald|Trade-off|~More boilerplate|no auto-injection|wire deps by hand|annotations are cleaner

sections.title: Manual Mock Creation Scenarios
When to Use Programmatic Mock Creation
sections.content:
Use **Mockito.mock()** when you need to create mocks in **@ParameterizedTest** methods where each test iteration needs a fresh mock with different configuration—annotations create one mock for all iterations.

Use it for **generic type mocking** like List<String> or Map<Long, Order> where you need to preserve type information that annotations can't capture.

Use it in **factory methods or test utilities** that generate test fixtures programmatically—you can't use @Mock in static helper methods.

Use it when **conditionally creating mocks** based on test data or environment flags—annotation-based mocks always exist, but sometimes you only want a mock under certain conditions. Finally, use it in **plain Java test classes** that don't use JUnit extensions, like integration test helpers or test data builders that create mocks as part of complex setup logic.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Not storing the mock reference**: Calling Mockito.mock(Service.class) but not assigning it to a variable, so you can't stub or verify it later—the mock is created and immediately garbage collected.
- **Mixing annotation and manual styles unnecessarily**: Using both @Mock at the class level and Mockito.mock() in @BeforeEach for the same dependency, creating two different mock instances and causing confusion about which one is actually injected.
- **Creating mocks in wrong scope**: Making a mock in one test method and trying to use it in another—each test method is isolated and doesn't share local variables, so the mock is null in the second test.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Mockito.mock(Class.class)**: Factory method that creates a mock object programmatically without annotation processing
- **Equivalent to @Mock**: Produces the exact same mock behavior as annotation-based mocks, just created manually
- **Generic type preservation**: Can mock List<String> or Map<Long, Order> and preserve type parameters at runtime
- **Dynamic creation**: Works in loops, conditional statements, or parameterized tests where annotations can't adapt
- **No MockitoExtension needed**: Works in any Java code, not just JUnit test classes with @ExtendWith
- **Helper method usage**: Perfect for test utility classes that generate mocks in static factory methods
- **Answer stubbing**: Supports withSettings() for advanced options like extra interfaces, serialization, or custom answers

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: To create a mock manually without annotations, you call Mockito.mock and pass in the class you want to mock, like Mockito.mock(PaymentGateway.class). That gives you a mock object right there in your code that works exactly like one created with the @Mock annotation. You'd use this style when annotations don't fit your situation. For example, in a parameterized test, you might need a different mock for each parameter value—you can't do that with @Mock because that creates one mock for the entire test class. Or if you're mocking a generic type like List of String, Mockito.mock lets you preserve that type information properly. Another scenario is when you're writing a helper method that builds test data—maybe you have a factory method that creates a fully configured order with mocked dependencies. You can't use @Mock inside a static utility method, but you can definitely call Mockito.mock there. The main trade-off is verbosity—manual mock creation is a bit wordier than just slapping @Mock on a field, but it gives you total control over when and how the mock is created. Most of the time, stick with @Mock for cleaner code, but know that Mockito.mock is there when you need the flexibility.

questions.question: How do you verify that a method was never called in Mockito?
questions.title: Mockito verify never() | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: Use verify(mock, never()).methodName(args) to assert a method was NOT called on a mock. Also use verifyNoInteractions(mock) to assert no methods were called at all. These are essential for testing negative scenarios like 'payment should not be processed when validation fails'.

interviewer_intent.testing: Do you understand negative testing and verifying that side effects don't happen inappropriately?
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Only knowing how to verify methods were called (positive verification), not knowing how to verify they weren't called.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give a concrete business scenario: when an order is cancelled, the inventory should NOT be decremented and the shipping service should NOT be called.

sections.title: Verifying Methods Were Never Called
sections.content:
**Negative verification** ensures that certain methods were NOT invoked, which is just as important as verifying they were called. Use **verify(mock, never()).methodName()** to assert a specific method was not called with given arguments. Use **verifyNoInteractions(mock)** to assert that absolutely no methods were called on the mock at all.

Think of it like a security checkpoint: positive verification checks that authorized actions happened, while negative verification checks that forbidden actions didn't happen. For example, if a payment fails validation, you need to verify the payment gateway was never charged—not just verify that the validation failed. Without negative verification, you might have a bug where both validation fails AND payment gets processed, and your test would miss it. This is especially critical for **side effects**: logging audit trails, sending emails, decrementing inventory, or calling external APIs. If your business logic says these shouldn't happen under certain conditions, your tests must explicitly verify they didn't happen, not just assume silence means correctness.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|never()|~Assert zero calls|verify mock never|method not invoked|guards side effects
blue|Alternatives|~Same intent|times zero|verifyNoInteractions|verifyNoMoreInteractions
emerald|Common Use|~Negative paths|no email on failure|no save on invalid|no retry when okay

sections.title: Negative Verification Examples
When to Use Negative Verification
sections.content:
Use **verify(never())** in **error path tests** where an early validation failure should prevent downstream side effects—like a failed credit check stopping payment processing.

Use it in **authorization tests** where an unauthorized user should trigger no write operations—verify no database updates, no API calls, no audit logs for the denied action.

Use **verifyNoInteractions()** when testing **circuit breaker or rate limiting logic**—when the circuit is open, verify the external service mock was never touched at all.

Use it in **conditional feature flag tests**—when a feature is disabled, verify that entire subsystems remain dormant.

Use negative verification to catch **regression bugs** where someone adds a new side effect to error handling code that shouldn't have side effects—your test will immediately fail when that unintended call happens.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Forgetting to test the negative case**: Only writing tests for the happy path where methods are called, never testing failure scenarios where methods should NOT be called—this leaves bugs undetected.
- **Using times(0) instead of never()**: Writing verify(mock, times(0)).method() which works but is less readable than verify(mock, never()).method() and doesn't signal intent as clearly.
- **Verifying wrong mock**: Calling verifyNoInteractions(wrongMock) instead of the mock that should actually be unused—typos in mock names cause false passing tests that don't verify anything.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **verify(mock, never()).method()**: Asserts the specified method was not called on the mock with the given arguments
- **verifyNoInteractions(mock)**: Asserts absolutely no methods were called on the mock—stricter than never()
- **Negative testing**: Explicitly verifying that side effects don't happen is as important as verifying they do happen
- **Error path coverage**: Essential for testing validation failures, authorization denials, and early-return logic
- **Side effect safety**: Guards against bugs where error handling code accidentally triggers actions it shouldn't
- **Argument matching**: Can use never() with argument matchers like anyString() to verify method wasn't called with any arguments
- **Multiple mocks**: Can call verifyNoInteractions(mock1, mock2, mock3) to check multiple mocks at once for cleaner test code

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: To verify a method was never called, you use verify with never mode, like verify(paymentGateway, never()).charge(anyDouble()). That asserts the charge method was not called at all during the test. There's also verifyNoInteractions which is even stricter—it checks that no methods whatsoever were called on the mock, which is useful when you want to confirm an entire subsystem stayed dormant. This kind of verification is crucial for negative testing—making sure things don't happen when they shouldn't. For example, imagine you're testing an order cancellation flow. When a user cancels their order, you need to verify that the shipping service was never called and the inventory was never decremented. Without that negative verification, you could have a bug where the cancellation happens but the shipping still gets scheduled, and your test would just check that the cancellation status is set correctly, missing the shipping bug entirely. The mistake freshers make is only testing the happy path where methods are supposed to be called, never testing the error paths where methods should stay silent. So if validation fails, you should verify that the downstream side effects like database writes or API calls never happened. That's the complete picture—positive verification for the happy path, negative verification for error paths and business rule violations.

questions.question: How do you set up Mockito in a Spring Boot project?
questions.title: Mockito Setup in Spring Boot
questions.direct_answer: Spring Boot's spring-boot-starter-test dependency includes Mockito (mockito-core and mockito-junit-jupiter) automatically. For pure unit tests, add @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class); for Spring context tests, use @MockBean instead. No manual Mockito dependencies needed.

interviewer_intent.testing: Do you understand how Mockito integrates with Spring Boot's test infrastructure without manual configuration?
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Manually adding mockito-core to pom.xml when it's already provided by spring-boot-starter-test, causing version conflicts.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Distinguish between mockito-core, mockito-junit-jupiter, and spring-boot-starter-test, and explain when @Mock vs @MockBean is appropriate.

sections.title: Mockito Integration in Spring Boot Projects
sections.content:
Spring Boot provides Mockito out of the box through the **spring-boot-starter-test** dependency, which is automatically included when you create a Spring Boot project from start.spring.io. This starter bundles **mockito-core** (the main library) and **mockito-junit-jupiter** (the JUnit 5 integration) together, so you get everything you need without manually managing Mockito versions. Think of spring-boot-starter-test as a curated test toolkit that gives you Mockito, JUnit 5, AssertJ, and other testing libraries in versions that are guaranteed to work together. For **pure unit tests** where you don't need the Spring context, you use standard Mockito with @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) and @Mock annotations. For **integration tests** where you do need Spring beans and the application context, you use Spring Boot's @SpringBootTest or @WebMvcTest with **@MockBean** to replace specific beans with mocks.

The key insight: Mockito is already there when you have spring-boot-starter-test in your pom.xml or build.gradle—you never add it separately.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Pure Unit Test|~No Spring context|the ExtendWith MockitoExtension|Mock plus InjectMocks|fast and isolated
blue|Slice / Integration|~Spring context loaded|the MockBean annotation|replaces a bean|slower startup
emerald|Dependency|~Already included|spring-boot-starter-test|test scope only|no manual add

sections.title: Mockito Setup in Spring Boot
When to Use Each Approach
sections.content:
Use **@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) with @Mock** for fast unit tests that test a single class in complete isolation—service layer logic, utility classes, or domain model behavior. These tests run in milliseconds because they don't start Spring.

Use **@SpringBootTest with @MockBean** when you need to test how components interact within the Spring container—controller-service-repository flows, bean autowiring, or configuration.

Use **@WebMvcTest with @MockBean** for focused controller tests that only load the web layer and mock out service dependencies.

Use **@DataJpaTest** when testing repository methods with a real in-memory database—Mockito isn't needed here because you're testing actual database interactions. The rule: if you can test it without Spring, use plain Mockito; if you need Spring's dependency injection or configuration, use @MockBean.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Adding mockito-core manually**: Declaring mockito-core as a separate dependency when spring-boot-starter-test already provides it, causing version conflicts where different parts of the test classpath use different Mockito versions.
- **Using @Mock in @SpringBootTest**: Trying to use @Mock and @InjectMocks in a Spring context test—Spring doesn't know about these annotations and won't inject the mocks into autowired beans.
- **Forgetting test scope**: Adding spring-boot-starter-test with compile or runtime scope instead of test scope, bundling testing libraries into production artifacts and bloating the final JAR.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **spring-boot-starter-test**: Bundles mockito-core, mockito-junit-jupiter, JUnit 5, AssertJ, and other test libraries in compatible versions
- **No manual setup**: Mockito is automatically available when spring-boot-starter-test is in your dependencies—no separate mockito-core needed
- **@Mock vs @MockBean**: @Mock for pure unit tests without Spring; @MockBean for integration tests that need the Spring context
- **Version management**: Spring Boot's BOM (bill of materials) ensures all test dependencies use compatible versions automatically
- **Scope test**: Always declare spring-boot-starter-test with scope test to keep it out of production artifacts
- **MockitoExtension**: Use this for unit tests; it has no Spring dependencies and starts tests instantly
- **@SpringBootTest overhead**: Full Spring context tests are 100-1000x slower than pure unit tests—use them only when necessary

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: In Spring Boot projects, you don't need to set up Mockito manually because it's already included in the spring-boot-starter-test dependency that comes with every Spring Boot project. That starter bundles Mockito core and the JUnit 5 integration together, so the moment you have spring-boot-starter-test in your pom.xml or build.gradle, you've got Mockito ready to use. For pure unit tests where you don't need Spring beans or the application context, you use regular Mockito with @ExtendWith MockitoExtension and @Mock annotations—these tests are super fast because they don't start Spring at all. But when you need to test something that requires the Spring context, like a REST controller with all its configuration, you use @SpringBootTest or @WebMvcTest and replace specific beans with @MockBean instead of @Mock. The difference is that @MockBean actually registers the mock in the Spring application context so it gets autowired into other beans, while @Mock just creates a standalone mock that Spring doesn't know about. The big mistake freshers make is manually adding mockito-core to their dependencies when it's already there from spring-boot-starter-test. That causes version conflicts because you end up with two different Mockito versions on the classpath. Just use spring-boot-starter-test with test scope, and you're all set—Mockito, JUnit, AssertJ, everything you need is already bundled and version-matched by Spring Boot.

sections.title: Comparing Programmatic and Annotation-Based Mock Creation
sections.content:
Mockito offers two ways to create mocks: **Mockito.mock(Class.class)** is the programmatic style where you call a factory method directly and get a mock object immediately. **@Mock** is the annotation style where you declare mocks as fields and let MockitoExtension initialize them during the test lifecycle.

Think of it like dependency injection patterns: programmatic mocking is like using new to create objects manually, while annotation-based mocking is like @Autowired where the framework wires things up for you. The annotation style is preferred in modern tests because it's **more declarative**—your test class clearly shows all dependencies at the top as annotated fields. It also integrates with **strict stubbing** by default when you use @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class), catching stale stubs automatically. The programmatic style gives you more control and works without JUnit extensions, but you lose the automatic lifecycle management and strict stubbing safety net unless you configure it manually.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Mockito.mock()|~Programmatic|called in code|returns a mock|works anywhere
blue|the Mock annotation|~Declarative|placed on a field|needs the extension|less boilerplate
emerald|Same Result|~Identical mock|choice is style|annotation for tests|method for dynamic

sections.title: Code Example
Mockito.mock() vs @Mock Annotation
sections.content:
| Aspect | Mockito.mock() | @Mock |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Initialization | Manual, in test method or setup | Automatic, by MockitoExtension |
| Declaration Location | Local variable or instance variable | Field annotation on test class |
| JUnit Dependency | None, works anywhere | Requires @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) |
| Strict Stubbing | Off by default, manual config needed | Enabled automatically by MockitoExtension |
| Readability | More verbose, creation mixed with logic | Cleaner, mocks declared at class level |

sections.title: When to Use Each Style
sections.content:
Use **@Mock** as your default for standard JUnit 5 tests—it's cleaner, safer with built-in strict stubbing, and makes test dependencies immediately visible at the top of the class.

Use **Mockito.mock()** when you need to create mocks conditionally or dynamically, like in parameterized tests where each iteration needs a different mock configuration.

Use the programmatic style in test utility methods or helper classes where annotations aren't processed, or when creating generic mocks like List<String> where type parameters matter.

Use @Mock when you want the full JUnit 5 lifecycle benefits: per-test mock initialization, automatic cleanup, and strict stubbing without manual configuration.

Use Mockito.mock() in plain Java code that doesn't extend JUnit test classes, like integration test setup scripts or test data factories.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using @Mock without @ExtendWith**: Declaring fields with @Mock but forgetting @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) on the test class—mocks remain null because nothing initializes them, causing NullPointerException on first use.
- **Mixing both styles unnecessarily**: Using @Mock at field level and then also calling Mockito.mock() in @BeforeEach for the same dependency, creating two separate mock instances and causing confusion.
- **Calling MockitoAnnotations.openMocks() redundantly**: Manually calling openMocks(this) in @BeforeEach when @ExtendWith already handles initialization—you initialize mocks twice, wasting resources and potentially causing subtle issues.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Mockito.mock()**: Factory method that returns a mock immediately, works anywhere in Java code without annotations
- **@Mock**: Field annotation that requires MockitoExtension to process and initialize before test methods run
- **MockitoExtension**: JUnit 5 extension that automatically initializes @Mock fields and enables strict stubbing by default
- **Lifecycle integration**: @Mock mocks are created fresh before each test; programmatic mocks live as long as their variable scope
- **Strict stubbing difference**: @ExtendWith enables STRICT_STUBS; Mockito.mock() uses LENIENT unless you configure otherwise
- **Readability**: Annotation style groups all test dependencies at the top; programmatic style scatters creation through code
- **Migration path**: Old JUnit 4 code using MockitoJUnitRunner can switch to @ExtendWith in JUnit 5 without changing mock declarations

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The main difference between Mockito.mock() and @Mock is how the mock gets created. With Mockito.mock(), you call it directly in your code—usually in a test method or in the before-each setup—and it gives you a mock object right there. With @Mock, you declare the mock as a field with the annotation, and MockitoExtension automatically initializes it before your test runs. You need to have @ExtendWith MockitoExtension at the class level for the @Mock annotation to work; otherwise, the field stays null and you'll get a NullPointerException when you try to use it. That's the most common mistake freshers make—putting @Mock on a field but forgetting the extension, and then being confused why the mock is null. The annotation style is generally preferred in modern tests because it's cleaner and more declarative—you can see all your test dependencies right at the top of the class as annotated fields. It also gives you strict stubbing automatically, which catches bugs where you declare stubs that never get called. The programmatic style with Mockito.mock() gives you more control and works in places where annotations don't, like inside parameterized tests or helper methods, but you lose the automatic lifecycle management and the strict stubbing safety net unless you configure that manually. So use @Mock as your default, and reach for Mockito.mock() when you need the flexibility or you're working outside the JUnit test class structure.

questions.question: What is strict stubbing mode in Mockito and why is it useful?
questions.title: Mockito Strict Stubbing | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: Strict stubbing mode fails tests if you declare a stub that is never called, or if the method is called with different arguments than you stubbed. It catches outdated or incorrect stubs, preventing test pollution. MockitoExtension enables STRICT_STUBS by default since Mockito 2.23.

interviewer_intent.testing: Do you understand advanced Mockito behavior that improves test quality, not just basic mocking?
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Getting UnnecessaryStubbingException and disabling strict stubs instead of fixing the test by removing the unused stub.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that strict stubbing is a quality gate that detects test drift when code changes but tests don't update their stubs.

sections.title: Understanding Strict Stubbing in Mockito
sections.content:
**Strict stubbing mode** is Mockito's built-in quality control system that actively looks for problems in your test setup. It enforces two rules: first, every stub you declare with when() must actually be called during the test—no dead stubs allowed. Second, if a method is called with arguments different from what you stubbed, Mockito immediately fails the test instead of silently returning null.

Think of it like a compiler for your test setup: just as Java won't compile if you declare a variable you never use, strict stubbing won't let your tests pass if you stub behavior that never executes. This catches a common test rot scenario—you refactor production code, the method signature changes, but old stub declarations remain in tests that now test nothing. Without strict stubbing, those tests keep passing but aren't actually validating anything anymore. Since Mockito 2.23, **MockitoExtension** enables strict stubbing by default, so you get this protection automatically in JUnit 5.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Strict Stubbing|~Default in JUnit 5|flags unused stubs|catches arg mismatch|UnnecessaryStubbingException
blue|Why It Helps|~Cleaner tests|removes dead setup|surfaces typos|self-documenting
emerald|Lenient Escape|~When you must|lenient() per stub|Strictness.LENIENT|use sparingly

sections.title: Strict Stubbing in Action
When Strict Stubbing Helps Most
sections.content:
Strict stubbing shines during **code refactoring** when you change method signatures or business logic—tests that should break because their stubs are now invalid will actually fail instead of passing silently. It's essential when **multiple developers work on the same codebase** and someone updates production code without updating all related tests; strict stubbing catches those orphaned stubs immediately.

Use it during **test reviews** to identify tests that are testing less than they appear to—if a test declares five stubs but only uses three, the other two are either dead code or indicate missing assertions. In legacy codebases with thousands of tests, strict stubbing acts as an automated cleanup tool that forces you to remove outdated test setup when you touch a test file.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Disabling strict stubs when seeing UnnecessaryStubbingException**: Adding lenient() or switching to lenient mode instead of fixing the actual problem—removing the unused stub or adding the missing assertion. The exception is telling you the test is broken; silencing it just hides technical debt.
- **Declaring stubs in @BeforeEach for optional scenarios**: Setting up stubs that only some tests need in a shared setup method—strict stubbing fails tests that don't use those stubs. Move stubs into individual test methods instead.
- **Copy-pasting test setup without cleanup**: Duplicating a test method, changing one line, but leaving all the original stubs intact—strict stubbing catches the now-irrelevant stubs that the new test doesn't exercise.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **UnnecessaryStubbingException**: Thrown when a test declares a stub with when() but never calls that method during execution
- **Argument mismatch detection**: Strict stubbing fails if production code calls a method with arguments different from the stubbed ones
- **Default in MockitoExtension**: JUnit 5 tests get strict stubbing automatically since Mockito 2.23—no configuration needed
- **Test drift detection**: Catches scenarios where code changes but tests don't update, leaving invalid stubs that pass silently
- **@MockitoSettings(strictness = LENIENT)**: Annotation to disable strict stubbing for a specific test class when truly necessary
- **lenient().when()**: Marks a specific stub as lenient if you need it for setup but can't guarantee it will be called
- **Production quality signal**: Teams with strict stubbing enabled consistently have fewer false-positive passing tests in CI pipelines

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Strict stubbing is Mockito's way of keeping your tests honest by failing them if you declare stubs that aren't actually used. Let's say you stub a method with when-then, but your test never calls that method—strict stubbing throws an UnnecessaryStubbingException to tell you something's wrong. It also catches cases where you stub a method with one set of arguments, like authorize with 100 dollars, but your code actually calls it with 200 dollars. Without strict stubbing, that would silently return null and your test might still pass even though it's not testing what you think it is. Since Mockito 2.23, strict stubbing is on by default when you use MockitoExtension in JUnit 5, so you get this protection automatically. The big mistake freshers make is seeing that exception, getting frustrated, and immediately adding lenient mode to make it go away. But that exception is actually helping you—it's saying either your stub is outdated and should be deleted, or your test is incomplete and you're missing an assertion. Think of it like a compiler error for your test setup. If you change production code but forget to update the tests, strict stubbing will catch those stale stubs and force you to fix them, which prevents test rot where tests pass but don't validate anything meaningful anymore.

questions.question: What does MockitoSession do and how does it differ from MockitoJUnitRunner?
questions.title: MockitoSession vs MockitoJUnitRunner
questions.direct_answer: MockitoSession is a programmatic, JUnit-agnostic way to initialize mocks and enforce strict stubbing; you call openSession and closeSession manually. MockitoJUnitRunner is a JUnit 4 runner that automates the same setup. In JUnit 5, use @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) instead of either.

interviewer_intent.testing: Do you understand different Mockito initialization approaches and when each applies, especially across JUnit versions?
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using MockitoJUnitRunner in a JUnit 5 project where it's not supported, causing runtime errors.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that MockitoSession is the low-level API used by extensions and runners, and is useful for framework-agnostic tests or custom test lifecycles.

sections.title: Understanding Mockito Initialization Mechanisms
sections.content:
**MockitoSession** is Mockito's low-level API for initializing mocks programmatically without depending on any test framework. You call **Mockito.mockitoSession()** to start a session, which initializes @Mock annotations and enables strict stubbing, then call **session.finishMocking()** to validate and clean up at the end.

Think of it as the engine under the hood that other tools use. **MockitoJUnitRunner** is a JUnit 4 runner (a @RunWith annotation) that wraps MockitoSession and automatically opens/closes it around each test. It's JUnit 4's way of integrating Mockito. In **JUnit 5**, you don't use runners anymore—the extension model replaced them. So you use **@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)** instead, which internally uses the same MockitoSession logic but integrates with JUnit 5's lifecycle. The relationship: MockitoSession is the foundation, runners and extensions are convenience wrappers for specific test frameworks. You'd use MockitoSession directly only in custom scenarios like non-JUnit tests, framework integration code, or when building your own test infrastructure.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|MockitoSession|~Manual lifecycle|startMocking()|finishMocking()|programmatic control
blue|vs MockitoExtension|~Extension is automatic|JUnit 5 wiring|no boilerplate|preferred default
emerald|When Session|~Non-JUnit runners|custom frameworks|fine-grained strictness|rare in practice

sections.title: MockitoSession vs JUnit Integration
When to Use Each Approach
sections.content:
Use **@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)** as your default for all new JUnit 5 projects—it's the modern, supported way to integrate Mockito.

Use **MockitoJUnitRunner** only if you're stuck on JUnit 4 in a legacy project and can't upgrade to JUnit 5.

Use **MockitoSession** directly when you're writing tests in a non-JUnit framework like TestNG, building custom test infrastructure, or integrating Mockito into a proprietary test harness.

Use it when you need fine-grained control over the mock lifecycle that doesn't align with standard test framework phases—for example, creating a long-lived session across multiple test-like operations in a test utility.

Use MockitoSession when writing library code that provides Mockito-based testing support to other developers, since you can't assume they're using JUnit.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using MockitoJUnitRunner in JUnit 5**: Trying to use @RunWith(MockitoJUnitRunner.class) in a JUnit 5 test class—JUnit 5 doesn't support runners, causing a runtime error that MockitoJUnitRunner is not found or ignored.
- **Forgetting to close MockitoSession**: Opening a session with startMocking() but never calling finishMocking(), which leaks resources and prevents strict stubbing validation from running.
- **Mixing initialization styles**: Using @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) and also manually creating a MockitoSession in @BeforeEach—you initialize mocks twice, which can cause subtle issues and is completely redundant.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **MockitoSession**: Low-level API for programmatic mock initialization and lifecycle management, framework-agnostic
- **MockitoJUnitRunner**: JUnit 4 runner that wraps MockitoSession to automate initialization before each test
- **@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)**: JUnit 5 extension that replaces runners, uses MockitoSession internally
- **JUnit 5 migration**: Replace @RunWith(MockitoJUnitRunner.class) with @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) when upgrading
- **finishMocking()**: Validates strict stubbing rules and releases resources—critical to call if using MockitoSession manually
- **Strictness configuration**: MockitoSession lets you set STRICT_STUBS, LENIENT, or WARN—extensions default to STRICT_STUBS
- **TestNG compatibility**: MockitoSession works with TestNG by calling it in @BeforeMethod and @AfterMethod hooks

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: MockitoSession is the core API that handles mock initialization and lifecycle management without depending on any specific test framework. You open a session manually by calling Mockito.mockitoSession(), which initializes your @Mock fields and turns on strict stubbing, and then you close it with finishMocking() when you're done. It's the foundation that other tools are built on. MockitoJUnitRunner is a JUnit 4 runner that wraps MockitoSession and automatically opens and closes it around each test method, so you don't have to manage the lifecycle yourself. But here's the thing—JUnit 4 is legacy at this point. In JUnit 5, the runner concept doesn't exist anymore; it was replaced by the extension model. So instead of MockitoJUnitRunner, you use @ExtendWith with MockitoExtension, which does the exact same job but integrates with JUnit 5's lifecycle. Internally, MockitoExtension is still using MockitoSession under the hood. You'd only use MockitoSession directly if you're writing tests in a framework other than JUnit, like TestNG, or if you're building custom test infrastructure that needs fine-grained control over the mock lifecycle. The mistake freshers make is trying to use MockitoJUnitRunner in a JUnit 5 project because they saw it in old tutorials. That doesn't work—JUnit 5 doesn't support runners. Just use @ExtendWith MockitoExtension for all your JUnit 5 tests, and you're covered.

questions.question: How do you reset or clear a mock between tests, and when is that necessary?
questions.title: Resetting Mocks Between Tests
questions.direct_answer: Use Mockito.reset(mock) to clear all stubbings and recorded interactions on a mock. However, this is usually a code smell indicating shared mock state across tests. The correct approach is to create fresh mocks per test using @Mock with proper test lifecycle, which MockitoExtension does automatically.

interviewer_intent.testing: Do you understand mock lifecycle, test isolation, and why shared mocks are an anti-pattern?
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Declaring mocks as static fields shared across all tests and then using Mockito.reset to clean them up between tests.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that needing Mockito.reset indicates a design problem with test isolation; the fix is per-test mock creation, not resetting shared state.

sections.title: Resetting Mocks and Test Isolation Principles
sections.content:
**Mockito.reset(mock)** wipes all stubbings and recorded interactions from a mock, returning it to a clean state as if it was just created. It sounds useful, but needing it is almost always a **test design smell**.

The core principle of good unit tests is **isolation**: each test should start fresh with no leftover state from previous tests. If you're sharing a mock across multiple tests and then resetting it, you're violating isolation—tests become order-dependent and harder to debug.

Think of it like washing dishes between meals instead of using clean plates: technically it works, but it's error-prone and you might miss a spot. The right approach is **per-test mock creation** with @Mock and @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class), which automatically gives you fresh mocks before each test method runs. MockitoExtension handles the lifecycle so you never think about resetting. The only legitimate use for reset() is in the rare case where you genuinely need to reuse a mock within a single test method—like testing behavior before and after reconfiguring a dependency—but even then, creating a second mock is usually clearer.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|reset(mock)|~Wipes stubs and calls|rarely needed|a code smell signal|prefer fresh mocks
blue|Better Default|~New mock per test|fields re-init|the extension handles it|isolated state
emerald|Legit Uses|~Long-lived spies|container-managed beans|partial cleanup|document why

sections.title: Anti-Pattern vs Correct Approach
When Reset Might Be Justified
sections.content: The **only legitimate use** for Mockito.reset() is within a single test method when you need to test behavior before and after reconfiguring a dependency—like verifying a service behaves differently when its data source fails and then recovers. Even then, creating two separate mocks is usually clearer. **Never use reset() to clean up between test methods**—that's what test isolation and per-test mock creation are for. If you find yourself wanting to reset mocks, ask: why am I sharing this mock across tests? The answer is almost always a mistake in test structure. In rare integration test scenarios where mock creation is extremely expensive and you're running hundreds of test operations in sequence, reset might save time, but that's not typical unit testing—and you'd still need careful documentation explaining why isolation was sacrificed.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Sharing mocks as static fields**: Declaring mocks as private static final or class-level variables shared across all test methods, then using reset() to clean them—this breaks test isolation and makes tests order-dependent.
- **Resetting in @AfterEach**: Calling Mockito.reset() in an after-each hook as a cleanup step instead of just creating fresh mocks per test—you're working harder to get worse isolation than the default behavior provides.
- **Resetting to fix test failures**: Seeing a test fail due to unexpected interactions and adding reset() to make it pass, without understanding why the interaction happened—reset masks the root cause instead of fixing the actual bug in test setup or production code.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Mockito.reset(mock)**: Clears all stubbings and recorded interactions, returning the mock to freshly-created state
- **Code smell indicator**: Needing reset() usually signals a test design problem with shared state or poor isolation
- **Proper isolation**: Use @Mock with @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) to get fresh mocks automatically before each test
- **Test order independence**: Per-test mock creation ensures tests can run in any order without affecting each other
- **Static mock anti-pattern**: Declaring mocks as static fields shared across all tests is a common source of flaky tests
- **Within-test reset**: The only valid use is resetting a mock within a single test method to test before/after behavior
- **Debugging difficulty**: Shared mocks with reset make test failures harder to diagnose because state leaks across test methods

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: You can reset a mock by calling Mockito.reset and passing in the mock object, which clears all the stubbings and interaction history on it. But here's the thing—if you're reaching for reset, that's usually a red flag that something's wrong with your test design. The need to reset a mock typically means you're sharing that mock across multiple test methods, and that breaks test isolation. Each test should start completely fresh with no leftover state from other tests, and MockitoExtension gives you that automatically by creating new mocks before each test runs. The anti-pattern looks like this: you declare a mock as a static field or a class-level instance variable that all tests share, and then you call Mockito.reset in an after-each hook to clean it up between tests. That seems like it works, but it makes your tests order-dependent and fragile—if one test forgets to reset, or if tests run in parallel, you get weird failures that are hard to debug. The correct approach is just to use @Mock on instance fields with @ExtendWith MockitoExtension, and the framework handles the lifecycle for you. Every test gets a brand new mock, so there's nothing to reset. The only time reset might be justified is within a single test method when you need to verify behavior before and after reconfiguring a dependency—like testing how a service behaves when its database connection fails and then recovers. But even then, creating two separate mocks is usually clearer than resetting one. Bottom line: if you find yourself calling Mockito.reset between tests, step back and restructure your test class to use per-test mock creation instead.
